meta.name: Machine Learning Interview Knowledge Base
meta.primary_source: Concept notes written from the topic structure of Tom Mitchell, 'Machine Learning' (McGraw-Hill, 1997). All summaries are original paraphrases written for this project; no book text is reproduced.

key_points: Define learning as improvement on task T under measure P as experience E grows.
The target function is what we want to learn; the hypothesis is the learner's approximation of it.
Choosing training experience (direct vs indirect feedback, teacher-provided or self-generated) shapes what can be learned.

questions.hint: T: classify emails as spam or not. P: fraction classified correctly (or precision/recall). E: a corpus of emails labelled spam/ham.
questions.q: How would you state a spam-filter project as a well-posed learning problem — what are T, P, and E?

questions.hint: Training data covers only part of the input space. The inductive learning hypothesis: a hypothesis that approximates the target well on a large enough set of examples will also approximate it on unseen examples.
questions.q: Why can a learner never be certain its hypothesis equals the true target function, and what assumption does inductive learning rest on?

chunks.summary: A learning problem is well posed when we can state the task T, the performance measure P, and the experience E the learner trains on. A program learns from E when its performance on T, measured by P, improves with E. Designing a learning system means choosing the training experience, the target function representation, and an approximation algorithm.
chunks.title: Well-posed learning problems

key_points: Bias = assumptions that let a learner prefer some hypotheses over others for unseen instances.
Examples: Occam's razor (prefer the simplest consistent hypothesis), nearest-neighbour smoothness, margin maximisation.
Bias is not avoidable; the design task is choosing bias that matches the problem.

questions.hint: Any learner that generalises must prefer some hypotheses over others on unseen data; that preference is its inductive bias. A purely unbiased learner can only memorise the training set.
questions.q: A colleague says their model has 'no bias — it just learns from data'. Why is that impossible?

questions.hint: A larger hypothesis space needs more data to pin down; stronger (more restrictive) bias effectively shrinks the space, reducing variance but risking systematic error if the bias excludes the target.
questions.q: How does inductive bias trade off against the size of the hypothesis space when training data is scarce?

chunks.summary: Inductive bias is the set of assumptions a learner uses to generalise beyond the training examples — for example, preferring shorter decision trees or smoother decision boundaries. Without bias, a learner can only memorise; with the wrong bias, it systematically misses the target concept.
chunks.title: Inductive bias

key_points: FIND-S finds a maximally specific hypothesis consistent with the positive examples.
The candidate-elimination algorithm maintains S and G boundaries and prunes them with each example.
The version space collapses to a single hypothesis when S and G converge; noisy data can collapse it to empty.

questions.hint: It minimally generalises the hypothesis — replacing mismatched attribute constraints with more general ones (e.g. a specific value becomes '?') — just enough to cover the example.
questions.q: What does the FIND-S algorithm do when it sees a new positive example that its current hypothesis does not cover?

questions.hint: FIND-S ignores negative examples and a single mislabelled positive can over-generalise it irreversibly. Candidate elimination uses both positive and negative examples to maintain the whole version space, so it degrades more gracefully and can detect inconsistency.
questions.q: Why does FIND-S fail on noisy training data, and what does candidate elimination do differently?

chunks.summary: Concept learning infers a boolean-valued function from positive and negative examples. FIND-S starts from the most specific hypothesis and generalises it only as much as each positive example forces, ignoring negative examples. The version space is the set of all hypotheses consistent with the training data, representable compactly by its most general (G) and most specific (S) boundary sets.
chunks.title: FIND-S and version spaces

key_points: Entropy H(S) = -p+ log2 p+ - p- log2 p- for a binary problem.
Information gain = entropy before the split minus the weighted entropy of the subsets after it.
ID3's bias is a preference for shorter trees with high-gain attributes near the root.

questions.hint: Entropy measures how mixed the class labels are in a set. Information gain is the expected drop in entropy from splitting on an attribute — the attribute with the highest gain is chosen because it purifies the subsets most.
questions.q: In your own words, what does entropy measure in a decision-tree split, and what information gain tells the algorithm?

questions.hint: Many-valued attributes fragment the data into tiny, pure subsets, inflating gain without generalising. Gain ratio corrects this by normalising gain by the split's own entropy (split information), as used in C4.5.
questions.q: Information gain is biased toward attributes with many distinct values, like a customer ID. Why, and what measure corrects for it?

chunks.summary: ID3 builds a decision tree top-down, at each node choosing the attribute that best separates the examples. 'Best' is measured by information gain: the expected reduction in entropy of the class label after splitting on that attribute. Entropy measures impurity — 0 for a pure set, maximal when classes are evenly mixed.
chunks.title: ID3, entropy and information gain

key_points: Overfitting: training accuracy keeps rising while true accuracy falls.
Reduced-error pruning uses a validation set to decide whether to replace a subtree with a leaf.
Rule post-pruning (as in C4.5) converts the tree to rules and prunes conditions, often generalising better.

questions.hint: The tree has likely memorised noise. Apply reduced-error pruning with a validation set (or limit depth/min-samples per leaf) and check whether test accuracy recovers while training accuracy drops slightly.
questions.q: Your decision tree reaches 99% training accuracy but 78% on the test set. Using the ideas of overfitting and pruning, what do you try first?

questions.hint: Generalisation depends on how well the hypothesis matches the underlying target, not the sample. Simpler trees have lower variance; a small rise in training error is worth it if the pruned tree tracks the true pattern instead of sample noise.
questions.q: Why can pruning a tree sometimes increase training error yet be the right thing to do? Frame your answer in terms of hypothesis complexity and unseen data.

chunks.summary: A hypothesis overfits when it fits the training data better than the target function, performing worse on unseen data — trees that grow until every leaf is pure often memorise noise. Remedies include stopping growth early and reduced-error pruning: grow the full tree, then prune nodes if removing them does not hurt accuracy on a held-out validation set.
chunks.title: Overfitting and pruning in trees

key_points: Perceptron learning converges if the data is linearly separable.
The delta rule uses gradient descent on squared error and converges to a best-fit approximation even for non-separable data.
Learning rate matters: too large oscillates or diverges, too small is slow.

questions.hint: A perceptron's decision boundary is a single straight line (hyperplane). XOR's positive and negative points cannot be separated by one line; it needs a hidden layer to form an intermediate representation.
questions.q: Why can a single perceptron learn AND and OR but never XOR?

questions.hint: The learning rate is too large, so each step overshoots the minimum and the error surface is traversed unstably. Reduce the learning rate (or add momentum/decay) and retrain.
questions.q: During training your loss oscillates wildly between epochs. What is the most likely cause in gradient-descent terms, and what do you adjust?

chunks.summary: A perceptron computes a weighted sum of its inputs and fires when it passes a threshold; it can represent linearly separable functions such as AND and OR but not XOR. Gradient descent searches weight space by following the negative gradient of an error function such as sum of squared errors, updating weights in small steps scaled by a learning rate.
chunks.title: Perceptrons and gradient descent

key_points: Chain rule: output error is distributed to hidden units in proportion to weights and unit derivatives.
Stochastic (per-example) updates often escape shallow local minima better than batch updates.
Overfitting in ANNs is controlled with weight decay, early stopping on a validation set, and more data.

questions.hint: It applies the chain rule: the error signal at an output unit is sent back along each connection weighted by that connection's strength and the derivative of the hidden unit's activation, so strongly connected, active hidden units receive more blame and bigger updates.
questions.q: Explain, without equations, how backpropagation decides how much each hidden unit contributed to the output error.

questions.hint: Poor weight initialisation (symmetry or saturated sigmoids), a local minimum of the error surface, and an inappropriate learning rate. Remedies: random restarts/different seeds, momentum, learning-rate schedules, or normalised inputs.
questions.q: Your network's training error plateaus early at a high value while a colleague's identical architecture trains fine. Give three distinct causes you would investigate.

chunks.summary: Backpropagation trains multilayer networks by computing the error at the outputs, then propagating blame backwards: each hidden unit is responsible for a fraction of the output error proportional to its connection weights. With sigmoid units the network can represent arbitrary continuous functions, but the error surface has local minima, so restarts, momentum, and weight initialisation matter.
chunks.title: Backpropagation and multilayer networks

key_points: Never estimate generalisation from the training set; it is optimistically biased.
k-fold cross-validation averages k holdout estimates and reduces variance of the estimate.
Differences between two algorithms on one small test set are often not statistically meaningful.

questions.hint: The model was optimised against that data, so sample error is biased downward; true error over unseen instances is what matters and needs held-out data to estimate.
questions.q: Why is accuracy measured on the training set not a trustworthy estimate of how a model will perform in production?

questions.hint: Whether the difference is statistically meaningful: with n=100 the standard error is about 3 points, so a 2-point gap is well inside noise. Use a larger test set or cross-validation with a paired comparison before concluding.
questions.q: Model A scores 91% and model B 89% on a 100-example test set. A teammate wants to ship A immediately. What do you check first?

chunks.summary: Sample error is measured on available data; true error is over the whole distribution of instances, and the two differ because of sampling variation. Honest estimates come from data the learner did not train on: holdout sets, and more efficiently k-fold cross-validation, which rotates the test fold so every example is tested once. Small samples give wide confidence intervals — roughly, error estimates from n examples carry uncertainty on the order of sqrt(p(1-p)/n).
chunks.title: Sample error, true error and cross-validation

key_points: Posterior ∝ likelihood × prior; the evidence term P(D) is a normalising constant.
MAP = ML when all hypotheses are equally likely a priori.
Bayesian methods can combine prior knowledge with data and output probability estimates, not just labels.

questions.hint: MAP maximises P(D|h)P(h) — likelihood weighted by the prior. ML maximises only P(D|h). They coincide when the prior over hypotheses is uniform.
questions.q: What is the difference between the MAP hypothesis and the maximum-likelihood hypothesis?

questions.hint: The prior P(disease) is tiny, so even a small false-positive rate applied to the huge healthy population produces more false positives than the true positives from the rare sick population. Posterior depends on base rates, not just test accuracy.
questions.q: A rare-disease test is 99% accurate, yet most positive results are false alarms. Explain this with Bayes' theorem.

chunks.summary: Bayesian learning treats hypotheses probabilistically. Bayes' theorem gives the posterior P(h|D) ∝ P(D|h) P(h). The maximum a posteriori (MAP) hypothesis is the most probable given the data and priors; maximum likelihood ignores the prior and picks the hypothesis that makes the observed data most probable. With enough data the prior's influence fades.
chunks.title: Bayes' theorem, MAP and maximum likelihood

key_points: Classify: argmax over classes of P(class) × product of P(attribute value | class).
Works well for text classification with thousands of word attributes.
Use smoothing so one unseen word does not zero out an entire class.

questions.hint: Classification only requires the true class to get the highest score; correlated evidence distorts the probability values but often preserves the ranking. The decision can be right even when the probability estimates are poor.
questions.q: Naive Bayes assumes attributes are independent given the class, which is false for text (words correlate). Why does it still classify documents well?

questions.hint: A zero conditional probability zeroes the whole product. Apply smoothing — e.g. add-one (Laplace) or an m-estimate — so unseen events get a small non-zero probability.
questions.q: A word in a test document never appeared in training for one class, and now that class scores exactly zero. What is the problem and the standard fix?

chunks.summary: Naive Bayes classifies by assuming all attributes are conditionally independent given the class, which reduces the joint likelihood to a product of per-attribute probabilities that are cheap to estimate. The independence assumption is usually false, yet the classifier is often competitive — because classification only needs the correct class to win the argmax, not accurate probabilities. Zero counts are handled with smoothing (e.g. Laplace/m-estimates).
chunks.title: Naive Bayes classifiers

key_points: Sample complexity grows with hypothesis-space capacity and with 1/ε and log(1/δ).
VC dimension of linear classifiers in d dimensions is d+1.
Theory formalises the intuition: simpler hypothesis spaces generalise from less data.

questions.hint: The lower-capacity model: PAC bounds say the gap between sample and true error grows with capacity, so for the same number of examples the simpler space has a tighter guarantee.
questions.q: Two models fit your training data equally well, but one has far higher VC dimension. All else equal, which do you expect to generalise better and why?

questions.hint: With probability at least 1-δ over the choice of training data, the algorithm outputs a hypothesis whose true error is at most ε — approximately correct, with high probability.
questions.q: What do ε and δ mean in the statement 'this algorithm PAC-learns the concept'?

chunks.summary: Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) learning asks how many examples a learner needs so that, with probability at least 1-δ, it finds a hypothesis with error at most ε. The VC dimension measures the capacity of a hypothesis space — the largest set of instances it can shatter (label in every possible way). Higher capacity needs more training data to guarantee the same error bound.
chunks.title: PAC learning and VC dimension

key_points: k-NN is lazy: no model is built at training time; cost is paid at prediction time.
Small k is noisy, large k over-smooths; k is usually tuned by cross-validation.
Normalise features, or large-scale attributes dominate the distance.

questions.hint: It does almost no work in training — it just stores examples — and defers computation to prediction, where each query must be compared against the stored set, making prediction slow on large data.
questions.q: Why is k-NN called a lazy learner, and what is the practical cost of that design?

questions.hint: The large-scale feature dominates the Euclidean distance, effectively deciding neighbours by itself. Standardise or normalise features so each contributes comparably (and consider dropping irrelevant attributes, which also distort distances).
questions.q: Your k-NN model performs terribly after you add a feature measured in thousands (e.g. salary) alongside features in 0–1 ranges. What happened?

chunks.summary: Instance-based learners such as k-NN store the training examples and classify a new point by the majority class of its k nearest neighbours under a distance metric — learning is deferred until query time ('lazy learning'). Performance hinges on the metric: irrelevant attributes distort distances, so feature scaling and selection matter, and accuracy degrades in high dimensions (the curse of dimensionality). Distance-weighted k-NN weights votes by inverse distance.
chunks.title: k-nearest neighbour and its pitfalls

key_points: Representation choice (how hypotheses are encoded) strongly affects GA performance.
Fitness-proportionate selection favours, but does not guarantee, survival of the fittest.
Crossover recombines building blocks; mutation maintains diversity.

questions.hint: When the objective is not differentiable or is discrete/combinatorial, the search space is rugged with many local optima, and evaluating a candidate is cheap — GAs need no gradient and explore broadly via a population.
questions.q: When would you reach for a genetic algorithm instead of gradient descent for an optimisation problem?

questions.hint: Crossover combines parts of two fit parents so good partial solutions (building blocks) can assemble into better wholes. Mutation introduces random variation, restoring diversity and letting the search reach regions selection alone would lose.
questions.q: What roles do crossover and mutation play in a genetic algorithm?

chunks.summary: Genetic algorithms search a hypothesis space by maintaining a population of candidate solutions (often bit strings), scoring each with a fitness function, and producing the next generation through selection of the fittest, crossover (splicing two parents) and mutation (random bit flips). They perform a parallel, stochastic beam search that can escape local optima that trap hill climbing.
chunks.title: Evolutionary search over hypotheses

key_points: Learn-one-rule, remove covered positives, repeat — a greedy set-cover strategy.
Beam search keeps the k best partial rules at each specialisation step.
Rules are interpretable, which makes them attractive where explanations matter.

questions.hint: It stops when the learned rules cover (nearly) all positive examples, or when the best new rule's quality falls below a threshold — each rule must earn its place by covering positives accurately.
questions.q: How does sequential covering decide when to stop adding rules to its rule set?

questions.hint: Interpretability: each rule is a standalone if-then statement a person can read, audit, and even edit, whereas a tree's meaning is spread across paths from the root.
questions.q: Give one practical advantage of a learned rule set over a decision tree for a business user.

chunks.summary: Rule learners such as sequential covering learn one rule at a time: find a rule that correctly covers many positive and few negative examples, remove the positives it covers, and repeat until most positives are explained. Rules are grown by adding conditions that maximise a quality measure (e.g. accuracy or an entropy-based score), then pruned to avoid overfitting. First-order (relational) versions like FOIL can express background relations that propositional rules cannot.
chunks.title: Sequential covering and rule quality

key_points: EBL generalises from one example by generalising its explanation, not the example itself.
Domain theories can be imperfect; combining them with data (KBANN, TangentProp-style methods) hedges that risk.
Prior knowledge effectively shrinks the hypothesis space the data must search.

questions.hint: It does not generalise the example's surface features; it generalises the proof of why the example is a positive instance, using the domain theory to identify which features were actually relevant. The knowledge does the work data does in induction.
questions.q: How can explanation-based learning generalise correctly from a single training example when inductive methods need thousands?

questions.hint: Hand-written domain theories are usually approximately correct, not perfect. KBANN encodes the theory as a network's starting point but still trains on data, so examples can correct the theory's errors.
questions.q: What problem with a purely knowledge-based system does KBANN's design address?

chunks.summary: Analytical learning uses prior domain knowledge, not just data. Explanation-based learning takes a single example plus a domain theory, builds a proof that the example satisfies the target concept, and generalises the proof into a rule that covers many similar cases. KBANN goes the other way: it translates a domain theory into the initial structure and weights of a neural network, then fine-tunes with backpropagation on examples — combining knowledge-driven and data-driven learning.
chunks.title: Explanation-based learning and KBANN

key_points: Credit assignment is the core difficulty: which earlier actions caused a later reward?
Q-learning update: Q(s,a) ← Q(s,a) + α[r + γ max Q(s',a') − Q(s,a)].
Exploration vs exploitation: ε-greedy policies occasionally try non-greedy actions to keep learning.

questions.hint: Supervised learning gets the correct label for each input immediately. RL gets only a scalar reward, often delayed, and must discover which actions in a sequence deserve credit — while its actions also change what data it sees next.
questions.q: How is reinforcement learning different from supervised learning, in terms of the feedback the learner receives?

questions.hint: Exploitation crowding out exploration: the agent keeps repeating its current best-known actions and never discovers better ones. ε-greedy action selection (or optimism/bonus terms) forces continued exploration.
questions.q: An RL agent converges to a mediocre strategy and stops improving. Which classic dilemma is this, and what mechanism addresses it?

chunks.summary: Reinforcement learning agents learn from sequences of actions and delayed rewards rather than labelled examples. In a Markov decision process the agent seeks a policy maximising cumulative discounted reward. Q-learning estimates the value of state-action pairs and updates them from observed rewards plus the discounted best next action, learning without a model of the environment; the discount factor γ trades immediate against future reward.
chunks.title: Q-learning, rewards and delayed credit
